If only you knew with certain knowledge﴾ ﴿You will surely see the Hellfire﴾ ﴿Again, you will surely see it with the eye of certainty﴾ ﴿Then on that Day you will surely be questioned about the bliss﴾.

As for its occasion of revelation (sabab al-nuzul), al-Kalbi and Muqatil narrated that there was a dispute (lihaa') between Banu Sahm and Banu Abd Manaf. They vied with each other in counting the living nobles, to see which of them was more numerous, and Banu Abd Manaf outnumbered them. Then they vied in counting the dead, and Banu Sahm outnumbered them, because they had been more numerous in the Jahiliyyah. Qatadah said: it was revealed concerning the Jews, who said: "We are more numerous than the family of so-and-so, and the family of so-and-so is more numerous than the family of so-and-so." Ibn Zayd said: it was revealed concerning a clan (batn) of the Ansar.

﴿Alhakum﴾ means "diverted you" (shaghalakum). According to what al-Kalbi and Muqatil narrated, the meaning is: you competed with one another in numbers of the living until you exhausted their count, and then you went to the graves and competed in numbers of the dead. He expressed their reaching the mention of the dead by "visiting the graves," as mockery of them. This meaning is one that the wording of "zurtum" (you visited) does not fit. It was said: ﴿until you visited﴾ means: you died and visited its graves with your bodies. That is, you cut short your lives with rivalry and boasting in wealth, children and numbers, until you died. Some Bedouin heard ﴿until you visited﴾ and said: "By the Lord of the Ka'bah, it has sent the people to the Resurrection, for the visitor departs and does not remain." Something similar to the Bedouin's saying is narrated from Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz. It was also said: this is a feminine (form) for the sake of frequent visiting, in order to honour those who have passed and to raise their remembrance.

The Messenger of Allah ﷺ had forbidden visiting graves, then he said: "so visit them" (fazurruha). This is a command of permissibility, for taking admonition from them, not for the purpose of boasting and vainglory. Ibn Attiyah said: "As people do in staying constantly by them, paving them with stones and marble, decorating them as a mark of honour, and building monuments (nawawis) over them." Ibn Attiyah had only seen the graves of the people of al-Andalus. How then would he be if he saw what the people of Egypt (Misr) boast of in their burial grounds at al-Qarafah al-Kubra, al-Qarafah al-Sughra, Bab al-Nasr, and elsewhere, and the wealth that is wasted there? He would marvel at that, and he would see what has not come to mind!

As for boasting in visitation, among those who attribute themselves to Sufism there are people whose only occupation is visiting graves. They mention regions they have traversed on foot in ascetic austerity (tajrid). They have memorised stories about the occupants of those graves and those shaykhs, so much that if they were written down they would fill volumes. Yet despite that, they do not know the obligatory acts of ablution (wudu') nor its sunnah. Kings and common people have been subjugated to them in good opinion of them and in giving them their wealth. As for whoever among them is an outlier and speaks to the common people and brings wonders, they say: "This is an opening (fath), this is from ladunni knowledge (al-'ilm al-ladunni), the knowledge of al-Khidr." Indeed, whoever attributes himself to knowledge, when he sees the popularity of this group, follows their path, transmits much of their stories, and mixes that with a little knowledge, seeking wealth, status, and the kissing of hands. The emphasis was increased by His saying ﴿with the eye of certainty﴾, to negate the suspicion of metaphor in the first seeing. Ali, Ibn Kathir in one narration, and Asim in one narration read it with a fathah in ﴿la-taruunna﴾ and a dammah in ﴿la-taruunnaha﴾. Mujahid, al-Ashhab, and Ibn Abi Abla read it with a dammah. They have made hamzah of incidental vowels that disappear in pausal pronunciation, such as ﴿istarwu al-salah﴾, so the hamzah of this is more appropriate.

From Ibn Mas'ud, al-Sha'bi, Sufyan, and Mujahid: it is security and health. From Ibn Abbas: the body and the senses, how they were used. From Ibn Jubayr: everything one takes pleasure in. In a hadith: "A house that shelters you, a garment that covers you, a morsel that sustains your heart, and whatever is beyond that is bliss."
